claims.text: Nickel-based superalloys are suitable for studying temperature-dependent plastic deformation.
The alloying chemistry of nickel-based superalloys can promote controlled plastic flow at elevated temperatures.
The elevated-temperature microstructural stability of nickel-based superalloys can improve creep resistance.
Forged and annealed nickel-based superalloys typically have an equiaxed grain microstructure at room temperature.
Elevated temperature enhances dislocation mobility in nickel-based superalloys.
Creep mechanisms become active at high service temperatures.
Grain-boundary characteristics regulate dislocation motion and creep deformation.
Precipitate distribution regulates dislocation motion and creep deformation.
Increased dislocation mobility at high temperature facilitates plastic deformation.
Diffusion-assisted creep processes at high temperature facilitate plastic deformation.
Stability imparted by alloying elements can delay grain-boundary weakening while maintaining mechanical integrity.
Under a temperature ramp, the material will exhibit increasing plastic deformation with increasing temperature.
Changes in strain rate will correspond to microstructural evolution and will be reproducibly measurable.
At room temperature, the superalloy exhibits minimal, primarily elastic deformation and negligible creep.
The proposed behavior applies only over the temperature range in which the microstructure remains stable.
Above a critical temperature, grain-boundary weakening and microstructural coarsening may cause uncontrolled deformation.
